entries.title: Where to start with: John Berger
entries.summary: The influential British writer and critic was born 100 years ago today. Here’s a guide to his genre-bending writing on art, love, sex, mortality and moreJohn Berger was born a hundred years ago today. He was an artist, critic, novelist, poet, polemicist and playwright who made impassioned, idiosyncratic, fiercely attentive and deeply humane contributions to a swathe of artistic and intellectual di
entries.content:
John Berger was born a hundred years ago today. He was an artist, critic, novelist, poet, polemicist and playwright who made impassioned, idiosyncratic, fiercely attentive and deeply humane contributions to a swathe of artistic and intellectual disciplines across six decades. In fact, the diversity of his output can make it “difficult to grasp,” as Geoff Dyer observes, in his introduction to the Selected Essays. “Even admirers tend to know him in only one or two of his many incarnations.”

I hope the recommendations below provide a somewhat representative handle on Berger’s range. I have limited myself to books he assembled himself, which means I haven’t allowed myself to include anthologies, such as the excellent Understanding a Photograph, edited by Dyer, or Tom Overton’s collections Landscapes and Portraits, or the recent selection Across a Frontier, chosen by the similarly interdisciplinary critic, photographer and novelist Teju Cole.

There are many ways to approach Berger, but wherever you choose to start, you will be encountering, as Susan Sontag said of him, “a wonderful artist and thinker”.

The entry point

Berger is best remembered for Ways of Seeing, his 1972 BBC television series and accompanying Penguin paperback. Radically, he combined art and social criticism, discussing artworks in relation to advertising, mass reproduction, the female nude, the male gaze and social status. The book’s format is equally revolutionary: the text appears to begin on the front cover, and three of the seven chapters are made up of images only. Ways of Seeing is a sui generis design classic and a swift introduction to Berger’s enduring preoccupations with art, sex and politics.

The prizewinner

The same year that Ways of Seeing was published, Berger won the fourth Booker prize with G. (1972). The novel itself has been somewhat overshadowed by Berger’s acceptance speech, in which he pilloried the sponsor Booker McConnell Ltd for their “extensive trading interests” in the Caribbean, announcing that he would be donating half his prize money to the British Black Panther movement. This experimental novel follows a young man (G) and his vigorous sex life as he travels across Europe on the eve of the first world war. G is mostly oblivious – but inextricably connected to – the world-historical events taking place around him.

The quiet masterpiece

Another excellent place to start would be A Fortunate Man (1967), the first collaboration between Berger and the Swiss photographer Jean Mohr. It is a deceptively simple portrait of a country GP in the Forest of Dean, told through stark photography and haunting prose. Word and image interweave to powerful effect: the minutiae of one man’s vocation reflect compellingly on the whole of society. Berger and Mohr became close friends working on this project and collaborated several times over the following 50 years.

The one for writers

One of Berger’s lesser-known titles is Photocopies (1996), which presents a series of exquisite prose vignettes, titled as if they were photographs. Berger captures real moments, reproducing them – photocopying them – with pinpoint attention to detail. The book has an air of delicate stillness: it is a masterclass in clarity and an inspiration for prose stylists.

The one for artists

Ways of Seeing may have made his name, but much of Berger’s best art criticism is collected in About Looking (1980), which includes essays on Turner, Giacometti, Magritte, Francis Bacon and Walt Disney. It also includes his famous essay Why Look at Animals?, which considers the fact that we rarely interact with animals today, despite living in a world full of animal imagery.

The best on photography

Berger’s third collaboration with Mohr was Another Way of Telling (1982), a revelatory investigation into the art of photography. Despite its diffident subtitle – “A Possible Theory of Photography” – this landmark work stands alongside those of Walter Benjamin, Roland Barthes and Susan Sontag. A photograph is “a meeting place,” writes Berger, “where the interests of the photographer, the photographed, the viewer and those who are using the photography are often contradictory”.

The best on politics

To some extent, everything Berger wrote was political; he was always concerned with the human experience in relation to society. One topic he wrote about repeatedly was migration, most memorably in A Seventh Man (1975), another remarkable collaboration with Mohr. This galvanising book intimately documents the experience of migrant labourers seeking work in western Europe in the early 1970s, but it remains soberingly topical today.

The one that will make you cry

G. may have won the Booker prize, but To the Wedding (1995) is Berger’s greatest novel. Through fragments of conversations, songs and silences, we follow a mother and father, estranged for many years, travelling across Europe to the wedding of their daughter Ninon. It’s both a heartbreaking story and a triumphantly optimistic celebration of love and life. Colum McCann calls it “one of the greatest and most honest love stories of our time.”

The one that deserves more attention

The wonderful Here Is Where We Meet (2005) is fiction – or is it? In 8½ chapters, “John” has a series of encounters with people who are dead: he meets his mother sitting on a park bench in Lisbon, he meets his childhood mentor in Krakow market, he stands above the grave of Jorge Luis Borges in Geneva. This is Berger at his most playful, seamlessly blending novel, essay, criticism, memoir and travelogue. It’s a brilliant, unclassifiable achievement.

The one to carry in your pocket

“This is a book I carry with me everywhere,” writes the actor and director Simon McBurney, in his new introduction to And Our Faces, My Heart, Brief as Photos (1984). “It fits into the inside pocket of my jacket, a little larger than a passport.” This slim, numinous work contains scraps and scenes about mortality, art, sex and belonging. It is organised into two halves – “Once”, about time, and “Here”, about space – and manages to condense a lifetime’s wisdom into little more than a hundred pages.

  • Henry Eliot edited the 2026 Bloomsbury reissues of John Berger’s work. He is the author of five books, including The Penguin Classics Book

entries.title: Winner of the Prix Goncourt literary prize admits to using AI
entries.summary: Philippe Jaenada told French radio that he used ChatGPT to ‘play with the reader’, after the prize removed a different book from its longlist over allegations of AI useThe winner of France’s most prestigious literary prize has admitted using artificial intelligence while writing his novel, barely a day after collecting an award whose jury had thrown out another book over suspected AI use.Philippe
entries.content:
The winner of France’s most prestigious literary prize has admitted using artificial intelligence while writing his novel, barely a day after collecting an award whose jury had thrown out another book over suspected AI use.

Philippe Jaenada, who won the Prix Goncourt on Tuesday for L’Inconnue du quai de Javel (The Unknown Woman of the Quai de Javel), told France Inter radio on Wednesday that he had turned to AI “three times” while writing it.

The first, he said, was to slip in a sentence written by ChatGPT in order to “play with the reader”. He said he had revealed which sentence it was only to the Goncourt jurors, on the day of the award. “If it gets out, I’ll know where it came from,” he said.

He also included a section of AI-generated text to poke fun at ChatGPT, which gave “completely absurd answers about a technical detail”, and for research.

“I don’t think AI can be held back. We can’t pretend it doesn’t exist,” said Jaenada, 62. “You have to use it – but first you have to acknowledge it, and above all you have to tame it. It has to be useful.”

The admission comes after the Académie Goncourt removed Thélyson Orélien’s book C’était ça ou Mourir (It Was That or Die) from its longlist in September. The Canadian-Haitian writer’s debut had been the breakout hit of France’s rentrée littéraire – the period between late August and early November which sees many books published in France – selling more than 35,000 copies and winning the Prix du roman Fnac (Fnac novel prize), before the journalist Samuel Fitoussi ran it through the AI-detection tool Pangram and concluded that much of it had been machine-generated. However, the accuracy of AI-detection software has been called into question.

In a statement on 25 September, the academy said analyses by researchers and journalists showed the novel was “in all likelihood very largely the product of an artificial intelligence”. It said it wanted to protect the integrity of a prize that exists to honour “literature written by women and men”, and to send “a clear message” that it did not endorse texts generated with the help of AI.

In an October statement, Orélien described the allegations as “slander and heresy”, adding that “not a single sentence in this book was created by a machine”. In the same statement, he admitted plagiarism in earlier work, apologising for claiming “as my own texts that are not mine”. The following week his Canadian publisher, Boréal, said new evidence showed AI had been used in the writing process, contrary to the author’s repeated assurances, and ended its relationship with him.

Jaenada had defended using AI before the award. “Would a film director hide the fact that he uses special effects?” he asked in an interview with 20 Minutes, predicting that it would soon be impossible to say a text was 100% human-written. But he insisted AI “will never be able to write a book with its heart, its soul, its memories”.

The contrast has prompted some accusations of a racial double standard online. “So when it’s an old white man it’s fine, but when it’s a young writer of colour he gets stoned in the public square?” one user wrote on X. Another said Jaenada had faced “no media lynching, no banishment” over his use of AI – “a leniency denied to Thélyson Orélien”.

Jaenada won on the first round of voting, by six votes to three over Sylvain Prudhomme’s De l’autre côté du lac (The Other Side of the Lake). Shortlisted four times before, Jaenada has made a speciality of reinvestigating old French crimes. His winning book reconstructs the unsolved 1949 murder of Louise Cansot, a 29-year-old Breton artists’ model known in Montparnasse as “the woman with 100 portraits”.

The prize itself comes with only a symbolic €10 cheque, but it is France’s best known and most closely watched literary award.

The Académie Goncourt, presided over by the novelist Philippe Claudel, has been approached for comment.

entries.title: American Hagwon by Min Jin Lee review – a gloriously immersive follow-up to Pachinko
entries.summary: A Korean family is willing to sacrifice everything for their children’s education, in the third book in Lee’s Diaspora Quartet“An excellent hagwon,” according to one of the characters in Min Jin Lee’s new novel, “is everything.” Every year, Korean parents pay hefty sums to send their children to these private after-school academies designed to turbocharge academic performance, where they spend eve
entries.content:
“An excellent hagwon,” according to one of the characters in Min Jin Lee’s new novel, “is everything.” Every year, Korean parents pay hefty sums to send their children to these private after-school academies designed to turbocharge academic performance, where they spend evenings and weekends being drilled in mathematics, reasoning and essay technique. In the third book in what she has called her Diaspora Quartet – a follow-up to 2017’s Pachinko, recently named one of the New York Times’s top 100 books of the 21st century – she presents the fierce competition to snag a spot at those hagwons deemed the best as symptomatic of Korea’s scarcity mindset: in a country where university places and white-collar jobs are hard to come by, everyone’s looking for an edge. But over the course of the novel’s 650 pages, they also come to stand as symbols of pretty much everything you can think of: of country and culture; of failure and success; of responsibility, or the lack of it; of what it means to achieve, and of what, in the final analysis, the purpose of our achievements might be.

The action in American Hagwon unspools over nearly three decades, and crisscrosses from Seoul to Sydney to California and back to Seoul again. At its centre is the Koh family: John, Helen and their three children, Bo, DH and Mido. When the novel opens in 1992, their life in Korea appears comfortably middle-class – John is a senior manager at a multinational corporation; Helen is an upmarket saleswoman, her commissions covering the children’s hagwon fees. But they are dramatically capsized: first by a personal betrayal and then again, in a brutal one-two, by the financial crisis that clobbered Asia in the late 90s. The family move, then later move once more: sometimes together, more often following their own trajectories; but always connected, and supporting one another as opportunity and need ebb and flow between them.

At every point, John and Helen put their children’s futures above their present comfort: education – seen as the surest route to security and self-worth – is prioritised above all else. In California, John fries fish and sluices the floors of the grandly named Shrimp Castle; Helen sells “imported face cream and handbags in a makeshift Korean department store that looked like a warehouse”. Every spare penny goes towards the astronomical expense of the trio’s academic careers: the essential which cannot be ducked.

This is, then, a family affair – but it soon becomes clear that, for Lee, the definition of family is elastic. The novel’s canvas is global, but the intertwined, intricate expat community it presents has the feel of a village. Friends, relatives and rivals move in close orbit, defined and bound together by their shared roots, their roles evolving as the years pass: sometimes bolstering one another with jobs and advice and connections, sometimes renewing decades-old feuds.

The novel’s expansiveness means that the people on the page come to appear as living, breathing beings – complex, contradictory, known intimately to each other but often unknowable themselves – to the point where being in their company feels like stepping into a longstanding family gathering. This is the novel as luxurious full-body experience: both in its patient tracking of the highs and lows of its characters’ lives, and in the compassionate realism with which it observes them, it reminded me of nothing so much as George Eliot’s Middlemarch – and, as with Eliot’s masterpiece, the effect of reading it is both immersive and transformative.

But it’s also, like Pachinko before it, a treatise on the Korean diaspora, and specifically on the role of the hagwon within it. When youngest child Mido finds work in the portentously named Fortress, a hagwon catering to the children of their southern California expat community, the novel tilts on its axis. Suddenly, we’re seeing the hagwon from the other side: not as supplicants at the fortress’s gate, but rather as its gatekeepers; guardians of the bright future it promises. Fortress was set up by Yun, Mido’s childhood friend from Seoul, and her husband Lion. Mido initially sees her work there as a stopgap, before she goes on to finish her own degree. But when she discovers that she loves the work, loves the children, and makes more than enough money to support herself she begins to wonder why she needs to return to university at all.

Lion, meanwhile, was a prodigy who graduated from Princeton in three years: exactly the sort of child hagwons are intended to produce. But rather than using his education as a springboard into the wider world, he has found himself running a hagwon of his own; drawn back to the system that launched him. And the trajectory of his own life, the experience of the children in his care, and the inherent injustices, of wealth and background, which the hagwon system perpetuates, leads him to question whether its ends justify its means. “There is a crisis … in our education and what it is meant to do,” he says to the parents of his students towards the novel’s end. “We cannot treat our students as objects to shape and bring to the market.” American Hagwon is a patient, humane, occasionally devastating book about what we ask our children to carry, and why.

entries.title: Feminism for a World on Fire by Natasha Walter audiobook review – an urgent call for collective action
entries.summary: The writer and activist finds galvanising energy in grassroots initiatives in the face of inequality and the climate crisis‘Throughout the world confidence in progress has shattered,” notes Natasha Walter. “The certainty – even the hope – that human rights equality might be within everyone’s reach has disintegrated … Everywhere in the world, from west to east, south to north, women are struggling
entries.content:
‘Throughout the world confidence in progress has shattered,” notes Natasha Walter. “The certainty – even the hope – that human rights equality might be within everyone’s reach has disintegrated … Everywhere in the world, from west to east, south to north, women are struggling to win and to protect their rights, and to live in safety. They keep coming up against misogynistic violence that never disappears.”

In Feminism for a World on Fire, Walter, an activist and academic, paints a dire picture of 21st-century womanhood. Where the last century saw women making strides towards equality, today much of that progress has been halted or gone into reverse. Social media, previously a place where women were able to come together and organise, now bubbles with hatred and misogyny. The impact of environmental catastrophe on the female population is stark: women are more likely to die from extreme weather events than men because they are more likely to be caring for children and elderly relatives. Meanwhile, male violence against women is rising and divisions in society, particularly over lightning-rod topics such as migration, are deepening.

But in the face of all this terribleness, Walter – who is the book’s warm yet authoritative narrator – finds women coming together in local communities and combating hardship and inequality through grassroots action and community initiatives. The author proposes shifting focus from individual female empowerment to collective action to bring about change. While Walter isn’t so glib as to suggest all will be well, her writing contains a galvanising energy: “If more and more people recognise the urgency of current challenges and step into action, the bigger changes may well occur.”

Available via Little, Brown 9hr 58min

Further listening

Hooked

Asako Yuzuki, 4th Estate, 13hr 35min

Ami Okumura Jones narrates the Butter author’s latest psychological thriller. Hooked features a young woman, Eriko, whose seemingly perfect life masks a loneliness which leads her to develop a fixation on a chaotic food blogger named Shoko.

Wants and Needs

Roxy Dunn, Fig Tree, 7hr 3min

Misty, a woman in her 30s, seems to have her life together until she finds herself single and living in her childhood bedroom. Then she meets a man through a dating app who proposes an unorthodox setup for a relationship. Read by the author.

entries.title: Alexander: God, King, Man by Edmund Richardson review – a dazzling, dizzying adventure
entries.summary: The winner of the 2026 Baillie Gifford prize is a riveting work of ancient history that feels startlingly present• ‘Blockbuster’ history of Alexander the Great wins £50,000 Baillie Gifford prizeIn 336BC, Alexander was not great. He was a wiry 20-year-old “no one had thought much about” who found himself king of Macedon after the assassination of his father, Philip. He seemed uniquely unfit for the
entries.content:
In 336BC, Alexander was not great. He was a wiry 20-year-old “no one had thought much about” who found himself king of Macedon after the assassination of his father, Philip. He seemed uniquely unfit for the position. Desperate to prove his worth, Alexander led an army into the Persian empire to confront Darius III, a man who ruled more than 50 million people. Darius was so confident of victory that he brought his family along for the show.

Alexander was outnumbered, and apparently out of his depth. He had suffered a fever that left him “shaking and helpless”, and dissent rattled through his ranks. A vast military force was bearing down on him, with Darius at the helm. “He did not know it yet,” Edmund Richardson writes, “but Alexander was about to become a legend.”

Alexander: God, King, Man is the story of that legend, told in dazzling and dizzying prose. It is the story of ruthless ambition, of restlessness leading to recklessness, of identity crises and messianic ideation, of a man who unleashed “violence on a scale never before seen”, conquering vast tracts of the world only to find himself paranoid and afraid. It is a story that, as Richardson shows, has been told by Roman politicians and Jewish scholars, by Icelandic bards and Persian courtiers. Which raises the question: do we really need another telling? In this case, yes. Partly because Richardson, professor of classics at Durham University, uses material from 12 languages, mining hieroglyphics, cuneiform and computer simulations, in a tremendous work of synthesis. And partly because his book is brilliant – and that is reason enough.

It is by necessity a violent read, tracking one conquest after the next, each battle characterised by some new brutality. But Richardson manages it with a light touch. The book frequently made me laugh amid the mayhem, and the author has a talent for selecting eye-catching details. At the battle of Issus, Alexander’s first confrontation with Darius, he introduces the phalanx: a 16-man-deep war machine, spiked with 19ft spears. We see the siege of Tyre through the lens of an engineer: it is a tale of catapults, boring machines, tridents and giant nests that “snatched up men” and “dashed them against rocks”. And we learn how Darius might have won the battle of Gaugamela, had he known horses could not stomach the stench of elephants.

It’s not all battles. On the march to Siwa, we observe the process of self-creation, as Alexander allows the Egyptians to designate him the son of their god, Amun. He may have let their adulation get the better of him, as he wrote in a letter: “King Alexander, the son of Zeus Amun, greets his mother, Olympias.” She responds, as only a mother could: “My dearest boy, don’t ever call yourself that again.” In Susa, we watch a drunk Alexander promising to pay off the debts of his soldiers, as well as dowries, a mistake Richardson calls “the most expensive hangover in history”. We follow him around Babylonia and witness a burgeoning existential crisis: is he king of Babylon or lord of the two lands? Is he son of Philip or Amun? Is he actually a god?

Richardson doesn’t mind diversions – flashing forward, flashing back, shifting through time and space. The book is all the better for it. The chapter on Alexandria and its library – a topic also covered in Richardson’s 2021 book, Alexandria: The Quest for the Lost City – is especially fascinating. The intellectual world centred on the library produced designs for the first ever steam engine, an early and close calculation of the world’s circumference, a flock of pneumatic singing mechanical birds and the first “universal” editions of Homer, achievements Richardson deems more wonderful than the literal wonders of the world. “Of all the ripples set in motion by Alexander’s life,” the author explains, “none have been as far reaching, and none continue to shape the world today, as much as the legacy of the Library.”

This is not the staid history of chalkboards but living, breathing history. It is a rush, and frequently hilarious. Speaking of the Greek contempt for their one-time enemies, Richardson says: “Persians were meant to be weak and uncivilised. Some of them even wore trousers.” The comic and the curious are often confined to brackets, interrupting the text but always welcome. “Amid vigorous linguistic competition … Greek’s fascination with the penis remains unrivalled.” Or better still: “Some survivors of the Trojan War were left behind … because, it was said, their buttocks had begun to rot. They settled in a new town called Pygela, which translates as ‘Ass City’.” Not all of the curiosities are as prurient, but they are always memorable.

Alexander’s life ends with a whimper, after so many spectacular bangs. He dies aged 32, battle-weary and fearing mortality, mourning the loss of his best friend, consumed by paranoia and consuming enough wine to drown an army. After so many near-deaths, he succumbs to a banal one, his killer salmonella typhi, likely contracted from river water. “The boy had become a king,” Richardson writes. “The king had become a hero. The hero had become a living god. Now … the god was dying, slobbering and broken-hearted, in Babylon.”

Despite its subject’s fate, Alexander: God, King, Man somehow sustains its sense of pace right up until the last word. It is a riot from start to finish, driven by exquisite prose and captivating stories, full of horror and violence, but laced with wonder and comedy.

Richardson shows us that you don’t have to sacrifice academic rigour at the altar of accessibility, and this exhaustively researched work will charm even the most general of general readers. It is a story about a long-disappeared empire, told with enormous verve and immediacy, and the biography of a man who forged a new world through force of will. “From the stars in the sky to the words on this page,” Richardson tells us, “Alexander reshaped reality more profoundly than almost anyone else in history.”

entries.title: Was one of the great novels of the Enlightenment written by a man who thought he was a werewolf?
entries.summary: Surreal, mysterious and with an outlandish origin story, Jan Potocki’s The Manuscript Found in Saragossa has amassed a cult following that includes Salman Rushdie and Jerry Garcia. But it’s the book’s global humanism makes it relevant now, say the curators of a new exhibitionA young Walloon officer called Alphonse van Worden travels through the Sierra Morena on his way to Madrid to join the Spanis
entries.content:
A young Walloon officer called Alphonse van Worden travels through the Sierra Morena on his way to Madrid to join the Spanish army. Along the way he has an erotic encounter with two demonic Moorish sisters, falls foul of shape-shifting apparitions and is tested by a Jewish Kabbalist attempting to use mystical formulas to control spirits and decipher the universe.

All these things happen in what might be one of the least-known great novels of the European canon, an encyclopedic roman-monde written more than 200 years ago called The Manuscript Found in Saragossa.

Structured like a Chinese box, with narratives nested within narratives, the book spans a period from the birth of Jesus Christ up to the beginning of the 19th century, and evokes places ranging from the Mediterranean and north Africa to Mexico, Peru and the Philippines. Salman Rushdie once described it in the Guardian as redolent of “the most brilliant modern novels, as if it were written yesterday”, while the curators of a new exhibition in Switzerland hail it as “a western version of One Thousand and One Nights”.

The fact that the book was written (in French) by a Polish count and the first fragments of it were published in 1804 in St Petersburg may explain why it remains relatively little-known in western Europe. That its globalised vision of unfettered human intercourse was dreamed up not in the familiar western European centres of colonial power – Paris and London – but the continent’s eastern reaches, however, may also be the reason why it’s attracting new attention now.

Its author, Jan Potocki (1761-1815), was born in Pików, in the Polish-Lithuanian commonwealth, but educated in Orbe, Switzerland – not far from the small village of Montricher where a newly opened exhibition at the Fondation Jan Michalski explores the books origins.“He was one of the very few Poles with a deep interest in Jewish culture as it was cultivated by rabbis in eastern Poland at the time, in what is now Ukraine,” says François Rosset, one of the two curators of The Manuscript Found in Saragossa: An Investigation into a World Novel. “This fascinated him and led him into the world of esoteric learning, including ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia.”

Potocki’s extraordinary life ended in 1815, when he shot himself at the age of 54. After his death, an inventory of his possessions at his Uładówka home revealed a silver sugar bowl with a missing lid. There is some speculation that an ailing Potocki filed down the knob of the lid to cast the bullet that killed him, sparking outlandish theories that he believed he was a werewolf.

The novel he left behind was to have an almost equally extraordinary afterlife. For many years, it circulated in fragmentary and competing versions. Among the most widely read was the English-language Penguin edition, beautifully translated by Ian Maclean, which was based on René Radrizzani’s revised French-language edition of 1990. But the notion that Radrizzani’s version represented the most faithful text was overturned in 2002, when the exhibition’s co-curator Dominique Triaire discovered eight manuscripts that had been miscataloged in Polish archives. “We were able to establish that Potocki had left behind not one but two novels,” Triaire says.

Potocki’s book has fervent admirers among contemporary novelists like the French Prix Goncourt winner Mathias Énard and Poland’s 2018 Nobel prize laureate Olga Tokarczuk, who has described it as part of her “literary first-aid kit”: “I open a page by chance and I draw a good dose of creative energy. All of the vital force of literature is there in its purest state.” But it’s fair to say that because of its inherent weirdness The Manuscript from Saragossa has never managed to establish itself as a classic of the European canon in the way that other roman-mondes such as Don Quixote or Boccaccio’s Decameron have. Yet, precisely because it is so open to interpretation, its influence on visual artists has been incredibly varied.

At the Swiss exhibition, a video screen shows the opening four minutes of Polish director Wojciech Has’s 1965 film adaptation of the novel, which brings all its surreal and comic qualities vividly to life, as soldiers run through the ruins of Saragossa to the strains of Beethoven’s Ode to Joy. The black-and-white film’s cult following helped inspire a restoration in the 1990s, initiated by the Grateful Dead’s Jerry Garcia and subsequently supported by Francis Ford Coppola and Martin Scorsese. Another screen shows excerpts of a four-part 1973 French television adaptation, La Duchesse d’Avila, which leans into a kitsch aesthetic underscoring the extraordinary elasticity of Potocki’s novel. Beyond the screen, the book also inspired 10 dreamlike engravings by Leonor Fini, who was commissioned in Buenos Aires in 1961 to produce illustrations for a rare bibliophiles’ edition.

To contemporary artists, it’s not just the fantastical world-building of Potocki’s book that appeals, but its vision of a globalised, multicultural society. The most recent is a theatrical adaptation directed by Grzegorz Jarzyna, which premiered at the Teatr Polski in Warsaw last year. The Saragossa Manuscript: The Gomelez Legacy is centred on Alex, a young inhabitant of a modern city, who travels back to 18th-century Spain only to be drawn into the machinations of a global secret society led by the Gomelez clan. In Potocki’s novel, the same Moorish family leads Alphonse on a merry dance of self-discovery, from a bumptious young officer steeped in received ideas into a man capable of thinking for himself.

“What Potocki wants Alphonse to acquire, and what makes The Saragossa Manuscript a novel of education, is a new set of values,” Triaire says. “Potocki was fundamentally an heir to the Enlightenment, for whom humanity was universal. There were no separate kinds of human beings divided by race or religion. White people, Black people, Christians, Muslims: these were all members of the same humanity.”

The novel’s principal setting of Spain’s Sierra Morena seems to have been chosen by Potocki to reflect a world without borders where everyone has a place at the table. In the novel, Alphonse encounters a stranger lying between the bodies of two hanged men (a recurring ghoulish motif) and helps revive him. Alphonse brings the man back to his camp where his Spanish hosts have arranged a breakfast. “A place had been kept for me. Another was laid for the stranger and no one asked who he was. Such are the laws of hospitality which are rarely broken in Spain.”

The novel’s treatment of religions is also notably modern. It suggests that the three great monotheistic religions can, in principle, coexist harmoniously, with the main characters often finding ways of understanding one another. The other is not to be feared. When the Spanish geometer Velásquez looks out over the ramparts of Ceuta and sees the vast territories inhabited by the Moors, he does not sense danger but the tranquillity of a pastoral landscape: “the countryside seemed to me to be there only to provide visual pleasure.”

There is, throughout the novel, a celebration of reason, but at the same time an acknowledgment of reason’s fragility. Potocki may have remained firmly committed to the Enlightenment, but its certainties were being shaken by the French Revolution and the Napoleonic wars. “It is through that crack in the edifice that something then described not as the fantastic, but as the supernatural, could enter,” Triaire says. “I think this fragility of reason also speaks to our own age.”

What gives The Manuscript Found in Saragossa such an enduring appeal, adds Rosset, is that its many layers reveal themselves differently to successive generations of readers. “He wrote a book that is outside time, but that belongs to all times.”

entries.title: ‘He was destined for this award’: China Miéville wins Goldsmiths prize for 1,200-page novel
entries.summary: The Rouse, which took its author two decades to complete, was praised by judges as ‘exuberant, overflowing’China Miéville has won the £10,000 Goldsmiths prize for The Rouse, a 1,264-page epic that is part paranormal thriller, part historical saga moving through decades of British imperial and cold war history.The win, announced at a ceremony in London on Wednesday, makes The Rouse the longest nove
entries.content:
China Miéville has won the £10,000 Goldsmiths prize for The Rouse, a 1,264-page epic that is part paranormal thriller, part historical saga moving through decades of British imperial and cold war history.

The win, announced at a ceremony in London on Wednesday, makes The Rouse the longest novel to take the prize since it was launched in 2013 to reward fiction that “breaks the mould or extends the possibilities of the novel form”.

The novelist Francis Spufford, who chaired the judges, said all the books on the shortlist were excellent, but “it seemed only right to give this year’s Goldsmiths prize to the one that, in terms of ambition, bold use of history, linguistic experiment and sheer scale, broke most explosively with expectation”.

Miéville has called The Rouse, which was 20 years in the writing, “the defining book of my life, that I’ve been writing for most of my adulthood” in an interview with the New Statesman, which co-founded the prize with Goldsmiths, University of London.

The novel opens in London in 1973 and follows Maur, whose son, Ewan, dies in an apparent suicide at an army barracks. As Maur tries to uncover what happened to her son, she finds allies among other bereaved families and a journalist, and gradually discovers the British state’s covert interest in the paranormal. Her search for the truth runs alongside the story of a soldier with experience of supernatural forces.

In a review for the Guardian, Stuart Kelly called it “maximalist, dense, disorienting and discomfiting”, arguing that Miéville deserves comparison with Roberto Bolaño and Mircea Cărtărescu, and describing the book as “affecting, intelligent and, in more than one place, very, very frightening”.

The novelist Hari Kunzru, one of the judges, called the book “a monumental work” in which Miéville “sets himself the daunting task of describing phenomena that are indescribable, stretching language to its limits and pushing formal and genre boundaries”.

“In a time when much fiction is careful to colour inside the lines, this enormous, exuberant, overflowing book is a reminder that the novel is capable of containing multitudes,” Kunzru added.

Tanjil Rashid, culture editor at the New Statesman, said Miéville had spent his career giving “imaginative form to a distinctly weird vision of the world, deeply personal but also unashamedly political”. He added: “Of all the awards he has won, this is the prize he was destined for.”

Miéville, who grew up in London, is known for novels including Perdido Street Station, The City & The City and Embassytown. He has won the Hugo, World Fantasy and Arthur C Clarke awards, and is a recipient of a Guggenheim fellowship. His nonfiction includes Between Equal Rights, a study of international law, and October, a history of the Russian Revolution. In 2024, he co-wrote a novel with the actor Keanu Reeves, The Book of Elsewhere.

Spufford was joined on the judging panel by the writer and translator Kate Briggs, Kunzru and the journalist and former Evening Standard literary editor David Sexton.

The Rouse beat five other shortlisted books: Polly Barton’s What Am I, a Deer?, Keith Ridgway’s Dooneen, Doireann Ní Ghríofa’s Said the Dead, Aea Varfis-van Warmelo’s Attention Seeking Behaviour and Missouri Williams’s The Vivisectors.

Now in its 14th year, the prize is open to novels by writers from, or resident in, the UK and Ireland that embody “the spirit of invention that characterises the novel genre at its best”. Last year’s prize was won by CD Rose for We Live Here Now. Previous winners include Rachel Cusk, Eimear McBride, Ali Smith, Isabel Waidner and Benjamin Myers.

entries.title: What we’re reading: Ian Rankin, Louise Kennedy and Guardian readers on the books they enjoyed in October
entries.summary: Writers and Guardian readers discuss the titles they have read over the last month. entries.content:
Ian Rankin, author

I’m a huge fan of Muriel Spark, but wasn’t sure I needed another biography of her, yet James Bailey’s Like a Cat Loves a Bird was a winning blend of detail and readability.

A Bad, Bad Place by Frances Crawford is a prize-winning debut crime novel set in 1970s Glasgow. It’s clever, authentic and humane with unforgettable protagonists and pitch-black humour.

The Heights by Ian Rankin is published by Orion (£25). To support the Guardian order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

David, Guardian reader

I’ve loved (most of) China Miéville’s books (I think that he and Alan Moore are the real doyens of “weird” fiction) – but The Rouse is surely his opus: sometimes prose-poetry, sometimes stream-of-consciousness, with shades (literally) of Lovecraft and MR James running through a bleak, unsettling yet compelling tale. I strongly suggest you take a very deep breath and launch into an adventure (lasting more than 1,200 pages) that will leave you dazed and amazed!

Louise Kennedy, author

I normally read one book at a time but, perhaps because I am on the road at the moment, I have three on the go. Emma Cline’s short story Arcadia almost killed me, and I’ve been a devotee ever since. Switzy, her new novel, accompanies on his final journey a man whose wealth and privilege offer no protection from the dementia that has begun to addle his poor brain. Edith Wharton’s The House of Mirth: so far, charming, pretty Lily Bart is in charge of her story, but an encounter with a man who appears not to wish her well suggests there may be trouble ahead. John McGahern’s Memoir already has my heart rent in twain, to paraphrase an old Irish ballad, and he hasn’t even finished primary school.

Stations by Louise Kennedy is published by Bloomsbury (£20). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

Sophie, Guardian reader

Almost Life by Kiran Millwood Hargrave is a beautiful and heartbreaking love story that transported me back in time to Paris in the late 1970s and 80s. The main characters, Laure and Erica, as well as the other characters, soon feel like friends – friends who are human and imperfect, and who sometimes make frustrating decisions, but who are all the more lovable for it. It’s elegantly and smartly written, and paints such vivid pictures – I rarely read past my bedtime these days, but I stayed up late for this one, torn between wanting to finish and never wanting the book to end. It captures the feeling of love and being in love so well.

Mark, Guardian reader

This year, I’ve set myself the challenge of only reading books by writers who aren’t part of the Anglosphere, with each writer being from a different country. It’s certainly forced me to read stuff outside my comfort zone – which is how, this month, I’ve ended up reading Independent People by Halldór Laxness, a 500+ page novel about an Icelandic farming family. Over the course of about 20 years in the early 20th century, we follow the hardships and privations of a stubborn farmer who insists he fend for himself to maintain independence on his own land.

I expected this book to be unrelentingly grim reading – and in parts it is, especially in the almost indifference to death. But it’s also very humorous in its characters’ cynicism towards one another. It’s beautifully atmospheric in its prose, particularly the changing of the seasons and their effect on the dramatic landscape of the farm. Reading so much literature in translation has given me an appreciation of when it’s done well (without ever knowing the original text), and the translation by JA Thompson, in collaboration with Laxness, is sublime.
